The Awaited Art of Async Programming in Python

The goal of this article is to help you build a strong mental model of asyncio.

It’s going to be legend .. a..

ryy!!

Let’s start by differentiating between synchronous code execution from asynchronous code execution

Difference between Synchronous Code Execution and Asynchronous Code Execution

I want you to think of the difference this way, synchronous code execution is the basic python code execution we are familiar with. This means code executes in a strict sequence and the running code blocks everything else until completion (blocking behavior); Example of Basic Python Function (Synchronous Code)

While for asynchronous code execution .. ? You guessed correctly! Asynchronous code execution does the opposite. It initiates tasks and continues without waiting for completion. Example of Asynchronous code

entry.title: How to build a self learning grok bot

link.title: How to build a self learning grok bot

entry.content:
How to build a self-improving grok bot

Grok bot is an autonomous AI system designed for ease and simplicity. I say this because by design you do not require technical expertise of any kind to create one.

When we talk about “self-improving”, the first question that comes to mind is how does self-improvement occur? The idea of self-improvement is very common to humans mainly because that’s all we have known & done throughout our lives. It’s simply after performing a task and having knowledge of what went wrong, you can make changes to either avoid the previous errors or overcome them on the next task. I mean you can relate it to writing a shell script or any script basically only after running the first time, then you know what changes to make. This is similar to grok bots they require feedback to self-improve.

Some key points to consider before creating one

  • What goal do you want the bot to achieve.
  • How do you evaluate completion of said goal.
  • How do you provide feedback.

For everyone who has used an AI chatbot or attempted creating an agent before you know the best approach is to be clear and explicit when providing your context and instructions. In that sense, grok bots are no different. One thing to be conscious of is grok bots are built to be proactive for example; the first thing the bot does once it is created is to predict its function or “goal” using its name, chat history and whatever information it has access to. Before providing instructions always ensure, you’ve thought through the steps and tools needed to achieve the goal. That’s there only way you can provide clear step by step instructions or create a skill needed by the bot to perform a task or accomplish a goal.

When it comes to how to evaluate the task and how to provide feedback. This is where you’re default bot comes in. I personally, feel like a lot of users under utilize their default bot. Your default bot can evaluate the task performed by the bot you created, grade the task and provide recommendations to help the bot self-improve.

Now let’s work through a simple demo task of creating a grok bot that finds AI fellowships programs on twitter.

The architecture is very easy:

When creating a new bot, you are provided with an option to name the bot and choose a profile icon. You can name the bot whatever you want, mine is named @ffinder.

Next step is to edit your bot’s profile to add a description and a title (optional).

Title: Research

Description: search X and find tweets on all fellowship posting related to AI, AI safety, AI Evaluation, AI Agent, AI Governance and AI research.

Next step: Send instructions to your bot;

1. search for tweets containing fellowships related to these AI areas: AI, AI safety, AI Evaluation, AI Agent, AI Governance and AI research.

2. Create a batch of your findings into a list

3. Forward batch to @controller (my default bot)

4. make this a weekly routine and run every Monday by 1pm

5. Do not duplicate findings.

Final step: Send these instructions to your default bot;

1. Inspect steps taken by @ffinder on AI fellowship research task.

2. Answer each evaluation question with Yes, No or Not sure.

3. Is the task completed?

4. Is each of the programs still accepting applications?

5. are the links provided the programs valid?

6. Evaluate and Score @ffinder based on these questions over 100.

7. Make recommendations to @ffinder on how to make improvements.

8. Notify me once the task is completed.

That’s it !! you’ve successfully created a self-improving grok bot

entry.title: How to build a Servicenow AI agent

link.title: How to build a Servicenow AI agent

entry.content:
So, how do you do it?

How do you build a servicenow AI agent?

Let’s say you wanted to build a servicenow AI agent. On a high level, here are a few things you should worry about; agent structure (name, description & instruction), triggers, ACL deployment and workflow configuration forrr ?? you guessed it - Agentic workflow.

So, let’s take a step back for a min and answer some basic questions.

What is a servicenow AI agent?

I mean… there are a lot of fancy definitions out there, using incredible words like: autonomous, artificial intelligence, & action.

Here is how you should look at it, AI = artificial intelligence (probabilistic computer intelligence) and agent = One that takes action.

Then we can say, an AI agent is a software program that utilizes artificial intelligence to take actions autonomously.

This is a fun architecture of an ai agent

We took the step back with hopes of you understanding that the logic is the same for servicnow ai agent under the hood. Now let’s look at a technical diagram of servicenow ai agent architecture components:

One thing you need to remember is servicenow comes with an ai agent orchestrator by default therefore the first hurdle to overcome is to avoid confusing the agent orchestrator. You can achieve that by ensuring that your agent’s name and description is unique and there are no agents pre-built or custom-built agents in your catalogue that performs the same function or similar functions as the agent you’re building.

Since you enjoy key points soo much, here are some more key points to consider when building a servicenow ai agent:

  • Authentication: You need to decide if the agent runs as a Dynamic user (Inherited Identity from user that invokes the agent or AI_User (service account Identity).
  • Trigger Config: Triggers are optional depending the workflow of the agent
  • Protection Policy: This determines who has access to make changes the agent. It like a resource lock if you have any experience with Microsoft azure.
  • Security ACL: This determines who has access to invoke the agent.
  • Tool Config: Tool configuration directly relates to the roles and instructions given to the agent. This means when defining your agent’s role, description and instruction you should also consider the tools the agent requires to perform those actions.

Now we are going to delve into something I call the etiquette of context. The Idea is simple, because artificial intelligence runs on natural-language, your definitions for the description, role and instructions given to the servicenow ai agent needs to be clear and explicit. These three fields are fundamentally important to the ability of your agent to perform tasks.

Field Purpose Answers
description Scope — what it DOES “What problem does this agent solve?”
agentRole Identity — what it IS (agents only) “Who am I?”
instructions Behavior — what it SHOULD DO “How should I act and use my tools?”

Note: Table from servicenow sdk official documentation (https://servicenow.github.io/sdk/guides/building-ai-agents-advanced-guide)

The writing principles are simply:

  • Use specific action verbs like fetch, retrieve, analyze, filter and update.
  • Reference tool explicitly in instruction
  • Add contingencies to handle failures or errors
  • Maintain coherence by ensuring each step in the instructions should builds on the previous step.
  • Tell the agent how to format outputs.

SideBar: Personally, when it comes to building a servicenow ai agent to complete a task. I feel it’s better when you’ve completed the task yourself at least once that way you can provide explicit step by step instructions when building the agent.

I believe you are ready to get your hands dirty; Here’s is a simple lab exercise to complete.
